newsitem.title: USA: US spot gasoline firm at late day, rumor churning.
newsitem.headline: US spot gasoline firm at late day, rumor churning.

text.p: U.S. spot gasoline prices remained firm in Houston late Thursday afternoon amid persistent rumors Exxon Corp was having problems at its large Baytown, Texas refinery near Houston.
"You've got to believe something was up," said one player who trades U.S. Gulf Coast gasoline who was seeking to explain a 3.50 cents upward explosion of U.S. Gulf gasoline prices.

The NYMEX move was 1.06, leaving the lion's share to USG cash diffs, which firmed by 2.50 cent in trade that saw prompt regular conventional gasoline get done at levels as high as 0.50 cent under the November NYMEX print.
The distillate market meanwhile headed south by 0.50 cent to 1.25 cents, tracking weaker NYMEX heat futures and softer diffs on heating oil, low sulphur diesel and jet fuel.

Traders said Colonial Pipeline's move earlier in the week to allocate space on its huge Houston-to-New York distillate line was again hurting distillate values since there appeared to be more barrels around than available space on Colonial.

Prompt USG heating oil got done at levels as weak as 3.85 and 3.90 cents under November NYMEX heat futures, with prompt USG low sulphur diesel and airline-grade jet fuel done at 2.25 and 2.60 cents under the November NYMEX print.
"I only see differentials softer," said one trader referring to his view of the likely ongoing effects of Colonial's allocation, which is set to be in effect through November.

On the gasoline front, traders appeared to be doubting Exxon's statements that all was operational at its huge 396,000 barrel per day (bpd) Baytown refinery, which includes 195,000 bpd of catalytic cracking capacity.

They also downplayed words by environmental regulators in both Texas and Louisiana that neither Baytown, nor any of the other plants involved in Thursday's rumor mill, were suffering from any problems serious enough to cause the companies to notify them of extraordinary air pollution emissions.
No matter how many or for what reasons refiners were buying gasoline in USG markets, all traders said Citgo was heavily involved.

Many traders thought Citgo's presence was perfectly logical, since Citgo is owned by state monopoly Petroleos de Venezuela SA, which is facing a downed cat cracker at its huge Amuay refinery in Venezuela.
"Amuay is why this market is flying," said one cash trader, referring to the refinery's stricken 108,000 bpd cat cracker, which he said exports as much as 60,000 bpd of gasoline to the United States.
That refinery unit will likely take three weeks to repair, traders and industry sources have said.
-- Oliver Ludwig New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1633
